claims.text: The initial material is a non-equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a disordered solid-solution structure.
Systematically varying constituent-element concentrations constitutes compositional tuning by atomic substitution.
Compositional tuning modifies local magnetic exchange interactions.
Compositional tuning modifies structural disorder.
Composition-dependent changes in local atomic arrangement and chemical short-range order alter magnetic exchange pathways.
Composition-dependent changes in local atomic arrangement and chemical short-range order alter interatomic distances.
Changes in composition adjust the valence electron concentration.
Composition-induced changes in valence electron concentration modify magnetic interactions.
Modified magnetic interactions change the magnetic ordering temperature.
Shifts in magnetic ordering influence the entropy change under an applied magnetic field.
Changes in field-induced entropy change modify the magnetocaloric response.
Systematic composition variation will produce a predictable shift in magnetic transition temperature.
Systematic composition variation will change the magnitude of the magnetocaloric effect.
The anticipated effects should be observable in low-dimensional HEA samples.
Results obtained in low-dimensional samples may not extend directly to bulk materials.
Results obtained for non-equiatomic alloys may not extend directly to nearly equiatomic alloys.
The direction of the proposed effects is supported by general principles of magnetic exchange in disordered alloys.
The precise magnitudes of the transition-temperature and magnetocaloric changes are uncertain without experimental calibration.
Failure to observe statistically significant transition-temperature shifts or magnetocaloric modulation beyond experimental error would falsify the hypothesis.
